summary:
The department of Vaupés stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Nationally, 13 trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, 41 trans women were killed in 2023, and eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024. The Millerey killing occurred in Antioquia, not Vaupés; its bearing on Vaupés is that lethal anti-trans violence can occur in daylight, be filmed, and leave the perpetrator unarrested.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Caquetá, armed groups have run a "social cleansing" campaign since at least July 2024, distributing flyers on the street and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets; a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend had been killed. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Discrimination limits trans women in these departments mainly to hairdressing or sex work. No Vaupés-specific finding appears in the source inventory.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
The organised-campaign pattern documented in Caquetá and Guajira is territorial rather than departmental: the actors are armed groups operating across several Colombian departments, and the flyer campaigns name trans people explicitly as military targets. A visitor to Vaupés should treat that as the relevant comparison class, since the inventory contains no evidence that such a campaign has been run in Vaupés itself, and equally no evidence that it has not.

The Millerey case is a single data point in a national count, not a Vaupés event: it occurred in Bello, Antioquia, and the national figures around it (13 trans people killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, 41 trans women killed in 2023, eight killed between February and April 2024) are the pattern the Vaupés assessment rests on.

Colombia's legal protections and its violence rates move in the same period rather than in sequence. The UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission praised the reforms while recording a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, which is the standing caveat on any reading of the country's formal framework as a predictor of street-level outcomes.

Conflict-era accountability is proceeding through a separate track from ordinary policing: the July 2023 indictments of 15 former rebels by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace addressed gender persecution as a crime against humanity, while the Millerey investigation had produced no arrest despite a presidential order. The two machinery types do not substitute for one another.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on government identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since June 2015; the 1993 Constitutional Court jurisprudence underpinning it requires no surgical procedure, and identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree imposes procedural obligations on government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and the May 2018 executive decree under President Juan Manuel Santos extends guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. These are resident-facing entitlements enforced through administrative channels rather than entry rules for visitors.

Custody conditions are governed by court order: a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a further ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

Discrimination in employment is documented as structurally narrowing: in the departments where armed-group campaigns have been recorded, trans women are limited mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and a trans woman who stood as a local election candidate in Caquetá was forced to flee after armed men gave her a week to leave town.

Residents in Guajira have been named on kill-list flyers posted by armed groups since March 2024, and in Caquetá flyers circulated by street and WhatsApp designate LGBTI people as legitimate military targets; the July 2023 Special Jurisdiction for Peace indictments recognised the conflict-driven version of this violence as gender persecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Vaupés-specific source appears in the inventory. Every finding above is national or drawn from other departments (Antioquia, Caquetá, Guajira), and the inventory states this explicitly for both the Millerey case and the Caquetá campaign. Whether armed-group flyer campaigns, kill lists or displacement orders operate inside Vaupés is unresolved and not sourced here.

The status of the comprehensive trans law pending before the legislature in 2025 is unresolved: the inventory records that it was under consideration, not that it passed or failed.

The inventory does not record whether the June 2015 notary route and the November 2025 "trans" and "non-binary" markers are administered identically in Vaupés's municipal registries, nor whether any Vaupés authority has issued its own LGBTI procedural decree beyond the 2016 Ministry of Interior and May 2018 presidential decrees.

Arrest status in the Millerey case is stated as of 14 April 2025 and may have moved since; the inventory carries no later update.

Whether the 2016 National Registry memo on registering same-sex marriages performed abroad has been applied without incident at designated offices in Vaupés is not sourced.
